Our purpose in one sentence: Silicofeller takes a quantum hardware engineer from a plain-language prompt to a fabrication-ready chip design. Four things make that possible: the platform is end to end, from research to tapeout; physics and verification are built in rather than bolted on; it supports multiple qubit architectures; and it is cloud native, so teams work on the same design together, with simulation running on GPU-accelerated cloud.

The problem · 1 of 2

How a quantum chip is designed today

Six steps, six different tools, and every hand-off is done manually. Steps 3 to 5 repeat until the numbers look right.

StepWhat engineers do by handToolsWhat goes wrong
1Write the designCode qubits, couplers and resonators line by line, with no picture of the chip.PythonQiskit MetalOverlaps and bend errors go unseen
2Export the geometryConvert the layout into CAD files (DXF / GDS) and clean up the polygons.CAD toolsLayer and polygon errors
3SimulateRebuild the model in a separate 3D solver and set up the mesh by hand.Ansys HFSSQ3DDays per run, workstations blocked
4Analyse resultsCopy frequencies and couplings into spreadsheets and custom scripts.ExcelMATLABCopy-paste mistakes, no single source of truth
5Fix and re-routeRedraw the waveguides by hand, then go back to step 3 and simulate again.PythonCAD toolsCrosstalk and impedance mismatch
6Fabricate and testWait for the cleanroom, then cool the chip down and measure it.FoundryCryostatFaults found only at the very end
silicofeller.com2
This is how most labs design a quantum chip today, step by step. One: an engineer writes the chip as code, hundreds of lines of Python, often in Qiskit Metal, with no picture of what they are drawing. Two: the geometry is exported into CAD files and cleaned up by hand. Three: the model is rebuilt in a separate 3D solver like Ansys HFSS or Q3D, where a single run can block a workstation for days. Four: the results are copied into Excel or MATLAB to work out frequencies and couplings. Five: the waveguides are redrawn by hand and the loop goes back to simulation, again and again. And six: the chip goes to the cleanroom, is cooled down and measured, and that is the first time anyone sees how it really behaves.

silicofeller.com3
Here is why that process breaks down. On the left is the real tool chain: KLayout, HFSS, Python, Excel, MATLAB, Qiskit Metal, and more, connected only by people moving files around. The result: a design cycle of around six months, more than ten tools per chip, days for every simulation, and most faults discovered only after fabrication, which means a respin. In a world where AI writes code and designs proteins, doing this by hand is the most expensive choice a hardware team can make.

silicofeller.com4
This is Silicofeller Quantum Studio. All seven tools become one studio that runs in the browser. You can start by simply describing the chip to our AI copilot, in plain language or as a target Hamiltonian, and it builds the design. You can refine it on a visual schematic editor with more than 58 pre-characterised components. Waveguides are routed automatically at 50 ohms with airbridges. Simulation, which used to mean rebuilding everything in HFSS, runs inside the platform: eigenmode, driven-modal, energy participation and capacitance extraction. On screen you can see a real driven-modal run. And when it is done, it is checked against design rules and surface-code requirements and exported as GDSII in one click.

silicofeller.com9
This is the difference, technique by technique. Chip design: today an engineer hand-writes Python in Qiskit Metal; in Silicofeller the AI copilot turns a target Hamiltonian into geometry. Layout and routing: KLayout and CAD tools, re-routed by hand, versus our schematic editor with automatic routing. EM simulation: in Ansys HFSS the model is rebuilt by hand and a run takes days; we run eigenmode and driven-modal simulation with the Palace FEM solver on the live design, in the cloud with GPU acceleration. Capacitance and quantum analysis: Q3D, pyEPR and spreadsheets, versus capacitance, EPR and Hamiltonian analysis in one workspace. Design-rule checks: today they run after export and faults show up after fabrication; ours run in real time. And tapeout: one-click GDSII with the Qiskit Metal code behind it. Net result: design cycles about ten times faster, by our own measurements.
